records.our_prose: Sugar snap peas are an edible-pod pea grown for plump, rounded pods eaten whole, pod and peas together, while the pod is still crisp, bright, and sweet. They are the plump-podded cousin of the flat snow pea: where a snow pea is picked young and flat before its seeds develop, a snap pea is left until the peas inside have swelled and nearly filled the pod, giving the crunchy, sugary pod that names the type. Like all peas they are a cool-season legume, sown as early as the ground can be worked in spring and again for a fall crop, and they fix much of their own nitrogen. Types range from tall climbing vines that need a trellis, such as the original Sugar Snap, to compact bush types like Sugar Ann that stand on their own; older varieties carry a string along the pod that is pulled off before eating, while newer ones are stringless.

records.our_prose: Sugar snap peas are ready when the pods have plumped up and rounded out, with the peas inside nearly full but the pod still bright green, crisp, and tender, roughly 5 to 8 days after flowering. Pick before the seeds bulge and stand out individually along the pod and before the pod dulls, yellows, or turns fibrous, the point at which it goes tough and starchy. Pick every one to three days: frequent picking keeps the vines flowering and producing, while overmature pods left on the plant signal it to stop. Snap the pod off with two hands so you do not tear the brittle vine, and pull the string along the seam of older, stringed varieties before eating.

records.our_prose: Across the cold northern tier sugar snap peas are a spring crop, with a second fall crop where the season allows. Sow as soon as the ground can be worked, even weeks before the last frost, since pea seedlings are cold-hardy; the spring crop is picked in late spring to early summer and then ends as midsummer heat stops the vines from filling pods and brings on powdery mildew. The hot weeks are left out, and a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop the frost-tolerant plants carry into autumn. From the milder end of the region (zone 7) a fall sowing can be grown through the cool months for a winter-into-spring harvest. The summer gap here is a true heat exclusion for peas, backed at each cell.

records.our_prose: St. George grows sugar snap peas on a single spring, direct-sown cycle, per USU Extension's "Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah," which sets Feb 15 as the St. George Group A (hardy) date for peas. Pods begin about 64 days later, and the tall indeterminate vines are pulled by early May, ahead of the 100°F heat St. George reaches from June into September. USU's table documents no fall pea window for St. George, so this cell runs a single spring cycle rather than a fabricated second one.

Make sure the lime is thoroughly mixed into the soil to a depth of 6-8 inches, then water the soil to promote the chemical reaction. If your soil pH is naturally above 7.0 (alkaline), where limestone, marl, or shells are present, there is no practical way of permanently lowering soil pH.
